lesson.title: Read a reaction as a ratio

lead.text: Go back to the pancake recipe: 2 eggs make 8 pancakes. Each egg is worth 4 pancakes, and that one fact is enough to cook any amount. Twenty pancakes need 20 ÷ 4 = 5 eggs, and forty need 10 eggs. The recipe stays the same while the size of the batch changes.

The comparison between the eggs and the pancakes is called a ratio. Here it is 2 to 8, which is the same as 1 to 4, and both ways of writing it describe the same recipe. Double both numbers and you get 4 eggs for 16 pancakes. Halve them and you get 1 egg for 4 pancakes. Whatever size you pick, the eggs and the pancakes stay in proportion.

A chemical equation holds a recipe of this kind. The ingredients are substances and the amounts are counted in moles. Reading the equation as a ratio is the first step in working out how much of one substance goes with another.

steps.headline: An equation is a recipe in moles

lead.text: Take the equation for making water, 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. Read it as a recipe and it says that 2 hydrogen molecules and 1 oxygen molecule make 2 molecules of water. The coefficients 2, 1 and 2 are the amounts, just as 2 and 8 were in the pancake recipe.

The recipe does not depend on how many molecules you cook. Make it twice over and you need 4 hydrogen molecules and 2 oxygen molecules to get 4 water molecules. Make it a dozen times over and the numbers are 24, 12 and 24. Each time, the three numbers are the coefficients multiplied by the same factor.

afterFigure.text: A mole is a count, so the recipe works for moles in the same way. Two moles of hydrogen go with 1 mol of oxygen and make 2 mol of water. Six moles of hydrogen go with 3 mol of oxygen and make 6 mol of water. The picture shows the recipe made once, twice and three times.
Read as amounts in moles, the coefficients of a balanced equation form the mole ratio of the reaction. For water the mole ratio is 2 : 1 : 2, whatever the scale.

lead.text: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen, following 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃. Read the coefficients as a recipe in moles.

steps.headline: Amounts the equation does not list

lead.text: So far the amounts you were given matched the equation exactly. Usually they do not. Suppose you have 6 mol of potassium and want to react it with bromine, following 2 K + Br₂ → 2 KBr. The equation says that 1 mol of Br₂ goes with every 2 mol of K, and that comparison is the ratio you scale with.

Write the ratio as a fraction with the substance you have underneath: 1 mol Br₂ over 2 mol K. Then multiply your amount by it, so 6 mol K × (1 mol Br₂ ÷ 2 mol K) = 3 mol Br₂. The mol K above and below the line cancel, which leaves moles of Br₂, the thing you wanted. A fraction used like this is a conversion factor, because it converts an amount of one substance into an amount of another. The pancake version is 20 pancakes × (2 eggs ÷ 8 pancakes) = 5 eggs.
These sums assume there is plenty of every other ingredient, so only the substance you start from sets the answer. Chemists say those other ingredients are in excess.
Nitrogen and hydrogen make ammonia, following N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. Hydrogen is in excess, so the nitrogen sets the amount of ammonia. Compare the two coefficients that matter and scale to your amount.

reveal.text: You scaled your 2 mol of nitrogen by the ratio of ammonia to nitrogen in the equation. Every calculation in this lesson works in that way.

steps.headline: For 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl, how many moles of Cl₂ are needed for 5 mol of Na?

workedSteps.text: Take the ratio from the coefficients: 1 Cl₂ for every 2 Na.
Multiply by a conversion factor with Na underneath, so the Na cancels.
workedSteps.math: 5 mol Na × (1 mol Cl₂ / 2 mol Na)

steps.headline: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of water form from 3 mol of O₂ with excess H₂?

workedSteps.text: The ratio is 2 mol H₂O for every 1 mol O₂.
workedSteps.math: 3 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O / 1 mol O₂)

workedSteps.text: Work out the amount of water.

steps.headline: Why the recipe is in moles

lead.text: Every calculation so far used moles, and that is deliberate. A mole counts molecules, so it lines up with the coefficients, which count molecules in the equation. Grams do not line up, because the molecules of different substances have different masses.

The water equation shows it. From the last lesson, hydrogen has a molar mass of 2 g/mol, oxygen 32 g/mol and water 18 g/mol. So 2 mol of H₂ weighs 2 × 2 = 4 g, 1 mol of O₂ weighs 32 g and 2 mol of H₂O weighs 2 × 18 = 36 g.

afterFigure.text: The masses 4 g, 32 g and 36 g do not follow the coefficients 2, 1 and 2, although they do add up, since 4 g + 32 g = 36 g. To use a mass in a reaction calculation, change it to moles first with n = m ÷ M. Apply the mole ratio to that amount. If you need grams at the end, use m = n × M.

lead.text: Magnesium burns in oxygen, following 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO. Write the ratio as a fraction with the substance you have underneath, then multiply.

steps.headline: Reading the ratio in either direction

lead.text: A reaction with several substances holds a ratio for every pair of them. Methane burns by CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, so methane and oxygen are in the ratio 1 to 2. Start from methane and every mole needs 2 mol of oxygen. Start from oxygen and the same pair reads the other way: every 2 mol of oxygen goes with 1 mol of methane, so you multiply by 1/2.

The coefficient of the substance you want goes on top of the fraction and the coefficient of the substance you have goes underneath. Swap the two substances and the fraction turns upside down. Products work like reactants. Water and methane are in the ratio 2 to 1, so 3 mol of methane burning makes 6 mol of water, and the same ratio takes you from a product back to the reactant it needed.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows one batch of methane burning and then two. Pick any two substances in it and their amounts keep the same ratio.

lead.text: A gas hob burns methane, and it needs enough oxygen to burn it. Start from the methane and find the oxygen it needs, using CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.

lesson.orientation: Use balanced coefficients to convert between reacting and produced amounts.
lesson.reviewLabel: Read a reaction as a ratio
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pancake recipe on the kitchen wall says that 2 eggs make 8 pancakes. Nobody has to cook exactly 8. If twenty people are coming, you work out how many eggs go with twenty pancakes, and the recipe still holds. It fixes how much of one thing goes with another, and you choose how many pancakes to make.

The last lesson ended with the idea that a balanced equation is a recipe too. 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O says that two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule make two molecules of water. Chemists rarely work with a handful of molecules. They work with moles, and a mole is only a count, so the same recipe can be scaled up to any number of moles you like.
This lesson reads an equation as a recipe in moles. Given an amount of one substance, you will work out how much of another it needs or makes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a balanced equation to say how many moles of one substance go with another.

recap.keyIdea: The coefficients of a balanced equation are a ratio of amounts in moles, not of masses. Multiply the amount you have by the coefficient ratio to find the amount you want.

blocks.text: Back in the kitchen, the eggs and the pancakes scaled together. The substances in an equation scale in the same way: 2 mol of N₂ gave 4 mol of NH₃, and 6 mol of Mg needed 3 mol of O₂.

recap.nextHook: Every one of those answers assumed there was plenty of every other ingredient. The next lesson asks what happens when one of them runs out first.

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ can 2 mol N₂ form with excess H₂?
hints: Which two coefficients compare ammonia with nitrogen?
How many moles of NH₃ does each mole of N₂ make?
Multiply the 2 mol of N₂ by that number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 mol N₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 1 mol N₂) = 4 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The equation gives two NH₃ for each N₂, so double the nitrogen amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The ratio of NH₃ to N₂ is more than one to one.
That is the amount of nitrogen. The equation gives more ammonia than nitrogen.

questions.prompt: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of water can 3 mol O₂ form with excess H₂?
hints: Each mole of oxygen supports two moles of water.
The equation gives two water moles per oxygen mole.
Evaluate 3 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The water-to-oxygen ratio is 2:1, giving 6 mol.

questions.onCorrect: 6 mol. Each O₂ makes two H₂O, so 3 mol of O₂ makes 3 × 2 = 6 mol.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the oxygen amount. Each O₂ makes more than one H₂O.
That divides by the ratio. Multiply by the ratio of water to oxygen.

questions.prompt: In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, the coefficients 1, 3 and 2 are a ratio between which quantities of the three substances?
hints: What does a mole measure, and what do the coefficients count?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coefficients count entities and amounts in moles; masses require molar masses.

questions.onCorrect: Coefficients are ratios of amounts in moles. Masses need the molar masses as well.

misconceptions.feedback: Grams need molar masses. Coefficients count amounts.
Coefficients say nothing about temperature.

questions.prompt: For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, how many moles of O₂ are required by 2 mol CH₄?
hints: Read oxygen required per methane consumed.
The oxygen-to-methane coefficient ratio is 2:1.
Evaluate 2 × 2/1.
questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The ratio is two O₂ for each CH₄, so double the methane amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The ratio is not one to one. Each CH₄ needs more than one O₂.
That is the methane amount. Scale it by the ratio.

questions.prompt: For 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, how many moles of MgO can 4 mol Mg form with excess oxygen?
hints: Reduce the product-to-reactant coefficient ratio.
The magnesium and magnesium oxide coefficients are both two.
Equal reactant and product coefficients keep the molar amount unchanged.
questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. The ratio of MgO to Mg is 1 : 1, so the amount is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the amount, but the Mg and MgO coefficients match.
That doubles the amount, but the Mg and MgO coefficients match.

questions.prompt: A stoichiometric calculation predicts 10 mol of product. When is this theoretical amount reached?
hints: Separate a theoretical calculation from actual reaction yield.

acceptedIdeas: When the stated reaction completes without competing losses
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The theoretical amount assumes the limiting reactant follows the stated reaction completely.

choices.label: When the stated reaction completes without competing losses
Only if all coefficients equal one

questions.onCorrect: A theoretical amount assumes the reaction goes as written, to completion and with no losses.

misconceptions.feedback: Balance is necessary, but real reactions can still lose product.
The coefficients can be any whole numbers. They do not set the yield.

questions.prompt: How many eggs do 20 pancakes need?
hints: How many pancakes does one egg make?
Then find how many eggs 20 pancakes need.
Divide 20 by the pancakes per egg, or scale the recipe.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 eggs make 8 pancakes, so one egg makes four. Then 20 ÷ 4 = 5 eggs.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A ratio scales: the same proportion holds for more or fewer. An equation's coefficients are a ratio like this.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the eggs by 5 without checking the ratio. Find how many eggs each pancake needs.
That multiplies the eggs by the pancakes. Use the ratio instead.

questions.prompt: In 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃, how many moles of Fe react with 3 mol of O₂?
hints: Which coefficient sits in front of Fe?
The coefficients are amounts in moles. Does 3 mol of O₂ match the O₂ coefficient exactly?
If 3 mol of O₂ is exactly one batch of the recipe, the Fe amount is the Fe coefficient.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficients are 4 for Fe and 3 for O₂, so 3 mol O₂ goes with 4 mol Fe.

questions.onCorrect: 4 mol. 3 mol of O₂ is exactly the recipe's amount, so Fe takes its coefficient.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount of O₂. The coefficient of Fe is different.
That is the Fe₂O₃ coefficient. The question asks about iron.

questions.prompt: Why is Na written underneath in the conversion factor?

acceptedIdeas: So the moles of Na cancel and the answer is in moles of Cl₂
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Na on the bottom cancels the Na on top.

choices.label: So the moles of Na cancel and the answer is in moles of Cl₂
Because sodium has the larger coefficient
Because the factor must always have the smaller number on top

questions.onCorrect: Right: put the unit you have underneath so it cancels and leaves the unit you want.

misconceptions.feedback: The position follows the units, not which coefficient is larger.
There is no rule about which number is larger. The units decide.

questions.prompt: For 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, how many moles of O₂ are needed for 6 mol of Mg?
hints: Compare the O₂ coefficient with the Mg coefficient.
There is one O₂ for every two Mg.
Multiply 6 by that ratio.
questions.onCorrect: 3 mol. One O₂ goes with each two Mg, so halve the magnesium amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount, but the ratio is one O₂ for every two Mg.
That is the magnesium amount. Scale it by the ratio.

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of H₂ are needed to make 4 mol of NH₃?
hints: Which two coefficients matter here?
Three H₂ go with two NH₃.
Multiply 4 by the ratio of H₂ to NH₃.
questions.onCorrect: 6 mol. The ratio is three H₂ for every two NH₃.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount, but the ratio of H₂ to NH₃ is not two to one.
That is the ammonia amount. Scale it by the ratio.
